title: De beiden Künigeskinner
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 113. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved exactly. This tale is in Low German (Plattdeutsch); the glossary gives the High German equivalent for each dialect form. The 1857 edition prints this tale without paragraph breaks; the paragraphing here is editorial, added for readability. The wording is unchanged.
about: KHM 113, told entirely in Low German, is a long, elaborate tale: a prince fated to be killed by a stag is rescued and hidden by a king's daughter, who helps him survive three nights of her father's deadly watch-riddles with the aid of a talking stone statue. A kiss from another woman then erases his memory of her entirely, and the princess must win him back through patient service and three magic walnuts before the true wedding can be held.

sentences.t: Et was mol en Künig west, de hadde en kleinen Jungen kregen, in den sin Teiken (Zeichen) hadde stahn,
sentences.l: It was once a king been, who had gotten a little boy, in whose sign it had stood,
sentences.i: There was once a king who had gotten a little boy, and in the boy’s birth-sign it had stood written
sentences.n: The whole tale is in Low German (Plattdeutsch), the North-German dialect the Grimms took it down in — not the High German of most tales — so nearly every word looks a little foreign: Et = ‘es’, was … west = ‘ist … gewesen’, mol = ‘mal’, en = ‘ein’, de = ‘der’, kregen = ‘gekriegt’, sin = ‘sein’, stahn = ‘gestanden’. Teiken is glossed (Zeichen) in round brackets by the Grimms themselves — the star-sign the child was born under. In the 1857 book this tale stands as a single unbroken column of type from first line to last; the paragraph breaks here have been added for the eye alone, and no word of the German has been moved.

sentences.t: he sull von einen Hirsch ümmebracht weren, wenn he sestein Johr alt wäre.
sentences.l: he should by a stag killed be, when he sixteen years old were.
sentences.i: he was to be killed by a stag when he turned sixteen.
sentences.n: sull = ‘sollte’; ümmebracht weren = ‘umgebracht werden’, literally to be brought around, i.e. killed; sestein = ‘sechzehn’; Johr = ‘Jahr’. The passive is built exactly as in High German, weren (werden) plus the past participle.

sentences.t: Ase he nu so wit anewassen was, do giengen de Jägers mol mit ünne up de Jagd.
sentences.l: As he now so far grown-up was, then went the huntsmen once with him on the hunt.
sentences.i: When he had grown that far, the huntsmen went out hunting with him one day.
sentences.n: Ase = ‘als’, when; anewassen = ‘angewachsen’, grown up; ünne = ‘ihm’. giengen is the 1857 spelling of gingen — gieng, fieng and hieng run all through the collection.

sentences.t: In den Holte, do kümmt de Künigssohn bie de anneren denne (von den andern weg), up einmol süht he do ein grooten Hirsch, den wull he scheiten, he kunn en awerst nig dreppen;
sentences.l: In the wood, there comes the king’s-son from the others away, all at once sees he there a great stag, that one wanted he to shoot, he could it however not hit;
sentences.i: In the wood the king’s son came away from the others; all at once he saw a great stag there, and he meant to shoot it, but he could not hit it;
sentences.n: Holte is ‘Holz’ in its older sense of a wood, not timber. denne carries its own round-bracket gloss from the Grimms, (von den andern weg), away from the others. scheiten = ‘schießen’; dreppen = ‘treffen’; awerst = ‘aber’. The tense slides from past into a vivid present (kümmt, süht) and back; this tale does that constantly.

sentences.t: up’t lest is de Hirsch so lange für ünne herut laupen, bis gans ut den Holte,
sentences.l: at the last is the stag so long before him out run, until quite out of the wood,
sentences.i: at last the stag ran on ahead of him so long that it drew him right out of the wood,
sentences.n: up’t lest = ‘aufs Letzte’, at last; für ünne herut = ‘vor ihm heraus’, out ahead of him; laupen = ‘gelaufen’. gans is ‘ganz’, quite — never a goose, though the spelling looks like one.

sentences.t: do steiht do up einmol so ein grot lank Mann stad des Hirsches, de segd „nu dat is gut, dat ik dik hewe;
sentences.l: there stands there all at once such a great tall man in place of the stag, who says “now that is good, that I you have;
sentences.i: and there all at once stood a great tall man in the stag’s place, who said, “Well now, it is good that I have you;
sentences.n: lank = ‘lang’, here tall; stad = ‘statt’, in place of; segd = ‘sagt’; dik = ‘dich’; hewe = ‘habe’.

sentences.t: ik hewe schon sess paar gleserne Schlitschau hinner die caput jaget un hewe dik nig kriegen könnt.“
sentences.l: I have already six pair of glass skates after you to-pieces hunted and have you not to get been able.”
sentences.i: I have already worn out six pairs of glass skates chasing after you, and have not been able to catch you.”
sentences.n: Schlitschau = ‘Schlittschuhe’, skates; caput jaget = ‘kaputt gejagt’, hunted to pieces; könnt = ‘gekonnt’, been able. Glass runs through the whole tale: the king will hand out a glass axe, a glass wedge and a glass spade, and every one of them shatters at the first stroke.

sentences.t: Do nümmet he ün mit sik un schlippet em dur ein grot Water bis für en grot Künigsschlott, da mut he mit an’n Disk un eten wat.
sentences.l: Then takes he him with himself and drags him through a great water up to before a great king’s-castle, there must he along to the table and eat something.
sentences.i: Then he took him along with him and dragged him through a great water as far as a great royal castle, and there he had to come to the table with him and eat something.
sentences.n: nümmet = ‘nimmt’; schlippet = ‘schleppt, schleift’; dur = ‘durch’; an’n Disk = ‘an den Tisch’. für here is ‘vor’, before — Low German för does the work of both vor and für, and this tale spells it für, fur and for by turns.

sentences.t: Ase se tosammen wat geeten hed, segd de Künig „ik hewe drei Döchter,
sentences.l: When they together something eaten had, says the king “I have three daughters,
sentences.i: When they had eaten something together, the king said, “I have three daughters;
sentences.n: geeten = ‘gegessen’; hed = ‘hatte’ (hebben = haben). Döchter = ‘Töchter’; the tale’s title calls the young people Künigeskinner, the king’s children.

sentences.t: bie der öllesten mußt du en Nacht waken, von des Obends niegen Uhr bis Morgen sesse, un ik kumme jedesmol, wenn de Klocke schlätt, sülwens un rope,
sentences.l: by the eldest must you one night watch, from of the evening nine o’clock until morning six, and I come every time, when the clock strikes, myself and call,
sentences.i: by the eldest you must keep watch one night, from nine of an evening until six in the morning; and every time the clock strikes I shall come myself and call,
sentences.n: des Obends is a genitive of time — “of an evening”. sülwens = ‘selbst’; schlätt = ‘schlägt’; rope = ‘rufe’. mußt keeps the 1857 ß (modern musst).

sentences.t: un wenn du mie dann kine Antwort gifst, so werst du Morgen ümmebracht, wenn du awerst mie immer Antwort givst, so salst du se tor Frugge hewen.“
sentences.l: and if you me then no answer give, so will you tomorrow killed be, if you however me always answer give, so shall you her as wife have.”
sentences.i: and if you then give me no answer, you will be put to death in the morning; but if you always answer me, you shall have her for your wife.”
sentences.n: kine = ‘keine’. gifst and givst are two spellings of ‘gibst’ inside a single sentence — the 1857 text does not regularise. salst = ‘sollst’; tor Frugge = ‘zur Frau’; hewen = ‘haben’.

sentences.t: Ase do die jungen Lude up de Schlopkammer kämen, do stund der en steineren Christoffel,
sentences.l: When then the young folk up to the sleeping-chamber came, there stood there a stone Christopher,
sentences.i: When the young people came up to the bedchamber, a stone Christopher was standing there,
sentences.n: Lude = ‘Leute’; Schlopkammer = ‘Schlafkammer’; stund = ‘stand’, stood. A steineren Christoffel is a carved figure of Saint Christopher; such statues stood in halls and doorways as house-guardians, and this one is about to answer the king in the young man’s place.

sentences.t: do segd de Künigsdochter to emme „um niegen Uhr kummet min Teite (Vater), alle Stunne bis et dreie schlätt, wenn he froget, so giwet gi em Antwort statt des Künigssuhns.“
sentences.l: there says the king’s-daughter to him “at nine o’clock comes my father, every hour until it three strikes, when he asks, then give you him answer instead of the king’s-son.”
sentences.i: and the king’s daughter said to it, “At nine o’clock my father will come, and every hour until it strikes three; when he asks, you answer him in the king’s son’s place.”
sentences.n: Teite is a northern nursery word for father, and the Grimms gloss it themselves in round brackets, (Vater). froget here is ‘fragt’, asks. giwet gi = ‘gebt ihr’ — gi is the plural ‘ihr’, used to the statue as a mark of courtesy. dreie = ‘drei’.

sentences.t: Do nickede de steinerne Christoffel mit den Koppe gans schwinne un dann jümmer lanksamer, bis he to leste wier stille stand.
sentences.l: Then nodded the stone Christopher with the head quite fast and then ever slower, until he at last again still stood.
sentences.i: Then the stone Christopher nodded his head very fast, and then slower and slower, until at last he stood still again.
sentences.n: schwinne = ‘geschwind’, fast; lanksamer = ‘langsamer’; to leste = ‘zuletzt’; jümmer = ‘immer’, ever. The nodding is the statue taking the charge on itself, and it will nod longer for each harder night.

sentences.t: Den anneren Morgen, da segd de Künig to emme „du hest dine Sacken gut macket,
sentences.l: The next morning, then says the king to him “you have your things well made,
sentences.i: The next morning the king said to him, “You have done your part well,
sentences.n: Den anneren Morgen is an accusative of time — on the next morning. hest = ‘hast’; dine Sacken = ‘deine Sachen’; macket = ‘gemacht’. sine Sacken gut macken is an idiom: to have done one’s job properly.

sentences.t: awerst mine Dochter kann ik nig hergiewen, du möstest dann en Nacht bie de tweiden Dochter wacken, dann will ik mie mal drup bedenken, ob du mine ölleste Dochter tor Frugge hewen kannst;
sentences.l: but my daughter can I not hand over, you would have to then one night by the second daughter watch, then will I myself once thereon consider, whether you my eldest daughter as wife have can;
sentences.i: but I cannot hand my daughter over; you would have to watch one night by the second daughter, and then I will think it over, whether you may have my eldest daughter for your wife;
sentences.n: hergiewen = ‘hergeben’, hand over; möstest = ‘müsstest’; sik drup bedenken = ‘sich darauf bedenken’, to think it over. The bargain has already shifted: the reward for tonight’s watch is only that he will consider the matter.

sentences.t: awerst ik kumme olle Stunne sülwenst, un wenn ik die rope, so antworte mie, un wenn ik die rope un du antwortest nig, so soll fleiten din Blaud für mie.“
sentences.l: but I come every hour myself, and when I you call, then answer me, and when I you call and you answer not, then shall flow your blood for me.”
sentences.i: but I shall come every hour myself, and when I call you, answer me; and when I call you and you do not answer, then your blood shall flow for me.”
sentences.n: olle = ‘alle’, here every; sülwenst = ‘selbst’; fleiten = ‘fließen’; Blaud = ‘Blut’. The threat is put with legal plainness, and the tale does not soften it.

sentences.t: Un do gengen de beiden up de Schlopkammer, do stand do noch en gröteren steineren Christoffel, dato seg de Künigsdochter „wenn min Teite frögt, so antworte du.“
sentences.l: And then went the two up to the sleeping-chamber, there stood there a still bigger stone Christopher, to that said the king’s-daughter “when my father asks, then answer you.”
sentences.i: And then the two went up to the bedchamber, and there stood a still bigger stone Christopher, and to it the king’s daughter said, “When my father asks, you answer.”
sentences.n: gengen = ‘gingen’; dato = ‘dazu’, to it; seg = ‘sagte’; frögt = ‘fragt’. Low German seg, seh and segd are all forms of seggen (‘sagen’) — a spelling that is easy to mistake for sehen.

sentences.t: Do nickede de grote steinerne Christoffel wier mit den Koppe gans schwinne un dann jümmer lanksamer, bis he to leste wier stille stand.
sentences.l: Then nodded the great stone Christopher again with the head quite fast and then ever slower, until he at last again still stood.
sentences.i: Then the great stone Christopher nodded his head again very fast, and then slower and slower, until at last he stood still again.
sentences.n: The sentence repeats the first night almost word for word; only grote, ‘große’, has been added. Formulaic repetition with a single word changed is this tale’s method throughout.

sentences.t: Un de Künigssohn legte sik up den Dörsüll (Thürschwelle), legte de Hand unner den Kopp un schläp inne.
sentences.l: And the king’s-son laid himself on the threshold, laid the hand under the head and slept in.
sentences.i: And the king’s son lay down on the threshold, laid his hand under his head, and fell asleep.
sentences.n: Dörsüll is glossed by the Grimms themselves as (Thürschwelle), the 1857 spelling of Türschwelle. schläp inne = ‘schlief ein’: inschlopen is separable and the particle stands at the end, as in einschlafen. Note also de Hand, not ‘seine Hand’ — a dative of possession, and German prefers it.

sentences.t: Den anneren Morgen seh de Künig to ünne „du hast dine Sacken twaren gut macket,
sentences.l: The next morning said the king to him “you have your things indeed well made,
sentences.i: The next morning the king said to him, “You have done your part well enough,
sentences.n: twaren = ‘zwar’, indeed, admittedly — it concedes the point before the ‘but’ that is coming. seh here is ‘sagte’, said.

sentences.t: awerst mine Dochter kann ik nig hergiewen, du möstest süs bie der jungesten Künigsdochter en Nacht wacken, dann will ik mie bedenken ob du mine tweide Dochter tor Frugge hewen kannst;
sentences.l: but my daughter can I not hand over, you would have to else by the youngest king’s-daughter one night watch, then will I myself consider whether you my second daughter as wife have can;
sentences.i: but I cannot hand my daughter over; you would have to watch one night more by the youngest king’s daughter, and then I will think it over, whether you may have my second daughter for your wife;
sentences.n: süs = ‘sonst’, otherwise, else. The bargain has slipped again: last night’s watch now buys only the second daughter, and the price of her is a third night.

sentences.t: awerst ik kumme olle Stunne sülwenst un wenn ik die rope, so antworte mie, un wenn ik die rope un du antwortest nig, so soll fleiten din Blaud für mie.“
sentences.l: but I come every hour myself and when I you call, then answer me, and when I you call and you answer not, then shall flow your blood for me.”
sentences.i: but I shall come every hour myself, and when I call you, answer me; and when I call you and you do not answer, then your blood shall flow for me.”
sentences.n: The threat comes back word for word, with only a comma dropped. The repetition is the point: nothing about the danger changes, only the price.

sentences.t: Do giengen se wier tohope (zusammen) up ehre Schlopkammer, do was do noch en viel grötern un viel längern Christoffel, ase bie de twei ersten.
sentences.l: Then went they again together up to their sleeping-chamber, there was there a much bigger and much taller Christopher, than by the two first.
sentences.i: Then they went up together to her bedchamber again, and there was a much bigger and much taller Christopher than at the first two.
sentences.n: tohope is glossed by the Grimms as (zusammen), together. ase does double duty: ‘als’ meaning when, and — as here — ‘als’ in a comparison, than. grötern, längern = ‘größeren, längeren’.

sentences.t: Dato segte de Künigsdochter „wenn min Teite röpet, so antworte du,“
sentences.l: To that said the king’s-daughter “when my father calls, then answer you,”
sentences.i: To it the king’s daughter said, “When my father calls, you answer,”
sentences.n: röpet = ‘ruft’; segte = ‘sagte’. dato = ‘dazu’, to it — the statue is addressed as a person.

sentences.t: do nickede de grote lange steinerne Christoffel wohl ene halwe Stunne mit den Koppe, bis de Kopp tolest wier stille stand.
sentences.l: there nodded the great tall stone Christopher a good half hour with the head, until the head at last again still stood.
sentences.i: and the great tall stone Christopher nodded his head a good half hour, until at last the head stood still again.
sentences.n: wohl here marks a full measure — a good half hour. halwe = ‘halbe’; tolest = ‘zuletzt’. Three nods, each longer than the last: a few beats, then longer, then half an hour.

sentences.t: Un de Künigssohn legte sik up de Dörsül un schläp inne.
sentences.l: And the king’s-son laid himself on the threshold and slept in.
sentences.i: And the king’s son lay down on the threshold and fell asleep.
sentences.n: Dörsül here, Dörsüll a few lines back: the 1857 text keeps both spellings and does not choose between them.

sentences.t: Den annern Morgen, do segd de Künig „du hast twaren gut wacket, awerst ik kann die nau mine Dochter nig giewen,
sentences.l: The next morning, then says the king “you have indeed well watched, but I can you still my daughter not give,
sentences.i: The next morning the king said, “You have kept watch well enough, but I still cannot give you my daughter,
sentences.n: nau = ‘noch’, still, yet — it turns up in every one of the king’s excuses. wacket = ‘gewacht’; twaren = ‘zwar’.

sentences.t: ik hewe so en groten Wall, wenn du mie den von hüte Morgen sesse bis Obends sesse afhoggest, so will ik mie drup bedenken.“
sentences.l: I have such a great wood, if you me it from today morning six until evening six hew off, then will I myself thereon consider.”
sentences.i: I have a great wood; if you cut it down for me from six this morning until six this evening, then I will think it over.”
sentences.n: Wall here is ‘Wald’, a wood — the Grimms themselves gloss the dative Walle as (Wald) further on. hüte = ‘heute’; afhoggest = ‘abhaust’, hew off, cut down.

sentences.t: Do dehe (that, d. i. gab) he ünne en gleserne Exe, en glesernen Kiel un en gleserne Holthacke midde.
sentences.l: Then did (that is, gave) he him a glass axe, a glass wedge and a glass wood-hatchet along.
sentences.i: Then he gave him a glass axe, a glass wedge and a glass wood-hatchet to take along.
sentences.n: dehe is ‘tat’, from dohn (= tun), and the Grimms explain it in their own round brackets: that, d. i. gab — “did, that is, gave”. Kiel here is ‘Keil’, a splitting wedge. midde = ‘mit’, the particle of mitgeben standing at the end.

sentences.t: Wie he in dat Holt kummen is, do hoggete he einmal to, do was de Exe entwei;
sentences.l: When he into the wood come is, there hewed he once at it, there was the axe in two;
sentences.i: When he had come into the wood, he struck one blow, and the axe was in two pieces;
sentences.n: hoggete … to = ‘hackte zu’, struck a blow — separable, with to at the end. entwei = ‘entzwei’, in two.

sentences.t: do nam he den Kiel un schlett einmal mit de Holthacke daruppe, do is et so kurt un so klein ase Grutt (Sand).
sentences.l: then took he the wedge and struck once with the wood-hatchet thereon, then is it so short and so small as grit (sand).
sentences.i: then he took the wedge and struck it once with the wood-hatchet, and it went as short and as small as grit.
sentences.n: schlett = ‘schlug’; daruppe = ‘darauf’. Grutt is grit or coarse groats, and the Grimms gloss it (Sand). so kurt un so klein — so short and so small — is the tale’s set phrase for smashed to nothing.

sentences.t: Do was he so bedröwet un glövte nu möste he sterwen, un he geit sitten un grient (weint).
sentences.l: Then was he so grieved and believed now must he die, and he goes to sit and weeps.
sentences.i: Then he was so downcast, and thought that now he must die, and he sat down and wept.
sentences.n: bedröwet = ‘betrübt’; glövte = ‘glaubte’; sterwen = ‘sterben’. grient is Low German grienen, and the Grimms gloss it (weint). geit sitten = ‘geht sitzen’, sits himself down.

sentences.t: Asset nu Middag is, do segd de Künig „eine von juck Mäken mott ünne wat to etten bringen.“
sentences.l: When it now midday is, then says the king “one of you girls must him something to eat bring.”
sentences.i: When it was now midday, the king said, “One of you girls must take him something to eat.”
sentences.n: Asset is ase + et, ‘als es’, with the pronoun written onto the conjunction. juck = ‘euch’; Mäken = ‘Mädchen’, here plural and unchanged in form.

sentences.t: „Nee,“ segged de beiden öllesten, „wie willt ün nicks bringen, wo he dat leste bie wacket het, de kann ün auck wat bringen.“
sentences.l: “No,” said the two eldest, “we want him nothing to bring, by whom he the last watched has, she can him also something bring.”
sentences.i: “No,” said the two eldest, “we will take him nothing; the one he watched by last can take him something too.”
sentences.n: wie is ‘wir’, we — not the English word it resembles, and not ‘wie’, how. willt = ‘wollen’; nicks = ‘nichts’; wo … bie = ‘wobei’, by whom; dat leste = ‘das letzte [Mal]’.

sentences.t: Do mutt de jungeste weg un bringen ünne wat to etten.
sentences.l: So must the youngest away and bring him something to eat.
sentences.i: So the youngest had to go and take him something to eat.
sentences.n: weg here means to be off, to set out; the verb of motion is simply left out, as it often is in this tale.

sentences.t: Ase in den Walle kummet, do frägt se ün wie et ünne gienge?
sentences.l: When [she] into the wood comes, then asks she him how it him went?
sentences.i: When she came into the wood, she asked him how things were going with him.
sentences.n: The subject se is missing from the first clause — Low German drops it freely — and it is supplied in square brackets in the literal line. Walle is the dative of Wall, ‘Wald’. wie here is ‘wie’, how — two lines earlier the same spelling was ‘wir’, we; wie et ünne gienge is a reported question, so the German keeps its question mark although the sentence is a statement.

sentences.t: „O,“ sehe he, „et gienge ün gans schlechte.“
sentences.l: “Oh,” said he, “it went him quite badly.”
sentences.i: “Oh,” he said, “it was going very badly with him.”
sentences.n: He answers about himself in the third person — ün, ‘ihm’ — because the narrator is reporting his words; this tale slips in and out of reported speech inside its own quotation marks. sehe = ‘sagte’; schlechte here is plain ‘schlecht’, badly.

sentences.t: Do sehe se he sull herkommen un etten eest en bitken;
sentences.l: Then said she he should come here and eat first a little bit;
sentences.i: Then she said he should come and eat a little first;
sentences.n: eest = ‘erst’, first; en bitken = ‘ein bisschen’; herkommen = ‘herkommen’, come over here.

sentences.t: „ene,“ sehe he, „dat künne he nig, he möste jo doch sterwen, etten wull he nig mehr.“
sentences.l: “no,” said he, “that could he not, he must indeed after all die, eat wanted he no more.”
sentences.i: “No,” he said, “that he could not do; he must die in any case, and he would eat no more.”
sentences.n: ene is a Low German ‘nein’. jo doch piles two particles together, ‘ja doch’ — after all, when all is said. Again he speaks of himself as ‘he’.

sentences.t: Do gav se ünne so viel gute Woore, he möchte et doch versöken: do kümmt he un ett wat.
sentences.l: Then gave she him so many good words, he might it after all try: then comes he and eats something.
sentences.i: Then she gave him so many fair words — he might try it after all — that he came and ate something.
sentences.n: gute Woore giewen, ‘gute Worte geben’, is a fixed phrase: to coax someone round with kind talk. versöken = ‘versuchen’; ett = ‘isst’.

sentences.t: Ase he wat getten hett, do sehe se „ik will die eest en bitken lusen, dann werst du annerst to Sinnen.“
sentences.l: When he something eaten has, then said she “I will you first a little louse, then become you otherwise in mind.”
sentences.i: When he had eaten something, she said, “I will pick the lice out of your hair a little first, and then you will be of another mind.”
sentences.n: lusen is ‘lausen’, to pick lice from someone’s head — an ordinary, intimate service in the world of these tales, and here the prelude to the magic. to Sinnen is the dative plural of Sinn: annerst to Sinnen werden = ‘anderen Sinnes werden’, to change one’s mind. getten = ‘gegessen’.

sentences.t: Do se ün luset, do werd he so möhe un schlöppet in,
sentences.l: As she him louses, there becomes he so weary and sleeps in,
sentences.i: As she picked the lice from his head, he grew so drowsy and fell asleep,
sentences.n: möhe = ‘müde’; schlöppet in = ‘schläft ein’.

sentences.t: un do nümmet se ehren Doock un binnet en Knupp do in, un schlätt ün dreimol up de Eere un segd „Arweggers, herut!“
sentences.l: and then takes she her cloth and ties a knot into it, and strikes it three times on the earth and says “earth-workers, out here!”
sentences.i: and then she took her kerchief and tied a knot in it, and struck it three times on the ground, and said, “Earth-workers, come out!”
sentences.n: ehren = ‘ihren’; Doock = ‘Tuch’, a cloth or kerchief; Knupp = ‘Knoten’; Eere = ‘Erde’. Arweggers is ‘Erdwerker’, earth-workers — the summoning word, and it will come back unchanged each time. A knotted cloth struck three times is the whole of her magic.

sentences.t: Do würen gliek so viele Eerdmännekens herfur kummen un hadden froget wat de Künigsdochter befelde.
sentences.l: Then were at once so many little earth-men come forth and had asked what the king’s-daughter commanded.
sentences.i: Then at once so many little earth-men came forth and asked what the king’s daughter commanded.
sentences.n: Eerdmännekens = ‘Erdmännchen’, little men of the earth. froget here is ‘gefragt’, asked. The pluperfect (würen … kummen, hadden froget) for a plain step in the story is a Low German habit; English needs a simple past.

sentences.t: Do seh se „in Tied von drei Stunnen mutt de grote Wall afhoggen un olle dat Holt in Höpen settet sien.“
sentences.l: Then said she “in time of three hours must the great wood hewn down and all the wood in heaps set be.”
sentences.i: Then she said, “Within three hours the great wood must be cut down and all the timber set in heaps.”
sentences.n: in Tied von = ‘in Zeit von’, within. Höpen = ‘Haufen’, heaps. The two halves of the passive, afhoggen … sien, stand far apart with the whole of the object between them.

sentences.t: Do giengen de Eerdmännekens herum un boen ehre ganse Verwanschap up, dat se ehnen an de Arweit helpen sullen.
sentences.l: Then went the little earth-men around and called their whole kindred up, that they them at the work should help.
sentences.i: Then the little earth-men went round and called up their whole kindred to help them at the work.
sentences.n: boen … up = ‘boten … auf’, called up, summoned (aufbieten). Verwanschap = ‘Verwandtschaft’, kin; Arweit = ‘Arbeit’; ehnen = ‘ihnen’.

sentences.t: Do fiengen se gliek an, un ase de drei Stunne ümme würen, do is olles to Enne (zu Ende) west: un do keimen se wier to der Künigsdochter un sehent ehr.
sentences.l: Then began they at once, and when the three hours around were, then is everything at an end been: and then came they again to the king’s-daughter and told her.
sentences.i: Then they began at once, and when the three hours were up, everything was finished; and then they came back to the king’s daughter and told her.
sentences.n: ümme sien = ‘um sein’, to be up, of time; the Grimms gloss to Enne as (zu Ende). sehent looks like a form of sehen, but the sense must be that they reported back to her, from seggen (‘sagen’) — the form is odd and the reading is not quite certain.

sentences.t: Do nümmet se wier ehren witten Doock un segd „Arweggers, nah Hus!“
sentences.l: Then takes she again her white cloth and says “earth-workers, home!”
sentences.i: Then she took her white kerchief again and said, “Earth-workers, home!”
sentences.n: witten = ‘weißen’, white. The dismissal balances the summons; both formulas stay fixed, and only nah Hus / to Hus varies.

sentences.t: Do siet se olle wier wege west.
sentences.l: Then are they all again away been.
sentences.i: And then they were all gone again.
sentences.n: siet is ‘sind’, are — not ‘Seite’, a side. wege = ‘weg’, away. The compound with sien again does the work of a plain past tense.

sentences.t: Do de Künigssohn upwacket, so werd he so frau, do segd se „wenn et nu sesse schloen het, so kumme nah Hus.“
sentences.l: When the king’s-son wakes up, then becomes he so glad, then said she “when it now six struck has, then come home.”
sentences.i: When the king’s son woke, he was so glad; and she said, “When it has struck six, come home.”
sentences.n: frau here is ‘froh’, glad — not ‘Frau’, a woman. upwacket = ‘wacht auf’; schloen = ‘geschlagen’; kumme = ‘komm’, an imperative.

sentences.t: Dat het he auck bevolget, un do frägt de Künig „hest du den Wall aawe (ab)?“
sentences.l: That has he also followed, and then asks the king “have you the wood off?”
sentences.i: That he did as she said, and then the king asked, “Have you the wood down?”
sentences.n: bevolget = ‘befolgt’, obeyed. aawe is ‘ab’, and the Grimms gloss it themselves; den Wall aawe [hewen] = to have the wood off, i.e. cleared. The verb is dropped, exactly as English drops it in “have you the wood down?”

sentences.t: „Jo“ segd de Künigssuhn.
sentences.l: “Yes” says the king’s-son.
sentences.i: “Yes,” said the king’s son.
sentences.n: Jo = ‘ja’. Note Künigssuhn here beside Künigssohn a few lines earlier — the 1857 text keeps both.

sentences.t: Ase se do an een Diske sittet, do seh de Künig „ik kann di nau mine Dochter nie tor Frugge giewen, he möste eest nau wat umme se dohen.“
sentences.l: As they then at one table sit, then said the king “I can you still my daughter not as wife give, he would have to first still something for her do.”
sentences.i: As they sat at one table, the king said, “I still cannot give you my daughter for a wife; he would have to do something more for her first.”
sentences.n: nie here is ‘nicht’, not — one of this tale’s standing traps, since the same spelling means ‘never’ in High German. The king begins by speaking to him (di) and ends by speaking about him (he) in the same breath. umme se dohen = ‘um sie tun’, do for her sake.

sentences.t: Do frägt he wat dat denn sien sulle.
sentences.l: Then asks he what that then be should.
sentences.i: Then he asked what that might be.
sentences.n: sien = ‘sein’, to be; sulle = ‘sollte’; denn is the particle that turns a plain question into an impatient one.

sentences.t: „Ik hewe so en grot Dieck,“ seh de Künig, „do most du den annern Morgen hünne un most en utschloen,
sentences.l: “I have such a great pond,” said the king, “there must you the next morning [go] over and must it out dig,
sentences.i: “I have a great pond,” said the king; “tomorrow morning you must go over there and dig it out,
sentences.n: Dieck = ‘Teich’, pond; hünne = ‘hin’, over there. The verb of motion is left out after most, as in High German ‘du musst hin’, and it is supplied in square brackets in the literal line. utschloen = ‘ausschlagen’, here to dig or clear out.

sentences.t: dat he so blank is ase en Spegel, un et müttet von ollerhand Fiske dorinne sien.“
sentences.l: so that it so bright is as a mirror, and there must of all kinds fish therein be.”
sentences.i: so that it is as bright as a mirror, and there must be fish of every kind in it.”
sentences.n: he refers back to the pond: Dieck is masculine, so Low German says ‘he’ where English says ‘it’. Spegel = ‘Spiegel’; ollerhand = ‘allerhand’; dorinne = ‘darin’.

sentences.t: Den anneren Morgen do gav ünne de Künig ene gleserne Schute (Schüppe) un segd „umme sess Uhr mot de Dieck ferrig sien.“
sentences.l: The next morning then gave him the king a glass spade and said “by six o’clock must the pond finished be.”
sentences.i: The next morning the king gave him a glass spade and said, “By six o’clock the pond must be finished.”
sentences.n: Schute is glossed by the Grimms themselves as (Schüppe), a shovel or spade. ferrig = ‘fertig’. Glass again: every tool the king hands over is made to break.

sentences.t: Do geit he weg, ase he bie den Dieck kummet, do stecket he mit de Schute in de Muhe (Moor, Sumpf), do brack se af:
sentences.l: Then goes he away, when he by the pond comes, there thrusts he with the spade into the mire (moor, swamp), there broke it off:
sentences.i: Then he went off, and when he came to the pond he thrust the spade into the mire, and it broke off short:
sentences.n: Muhe carries the Grimms’ own gloss, (Moor, Sumpf) — boggy ground. brack af = ‘brach ab’; stecket = ‘steckt, sticht’.

sentences.t: do stecket he mit de Hacken in de Muhe, un et was wier caput.
sentences.l: then thrusts he with the mattock into the mire, and it was again broken.
sentences.i: then he thrust in with the mattock, and that was broken too.
sentences.n: Hacken is the dative of Hacke, a mattock or hoe. caput = ‘kaputt’, in the older spelling the 1857 text uses.

sentences.t: Do werd he gans bedröwet.
sentences.l: Then becomes he quite downcast.
sentences.i: Then he was utterly downcast.
sentences.n: gans = ‘ganz’, quite, utterly — the tale’s favourite intensifier.

sentences.t: Den Middag brachte de jüngeste Dochter ünne wat to etten, do frägt se wo et ünne gienge?
sentences.l: At midday brought the youngest daughter him something to eat, then asks she how it him went?
sentences.i: At midday the youngest daughter brought him something to eat, and asked how things were going with him.
sentences.n: Den Middag is again an accusative of time. wo is ‘wie’, how; Low German uses wo for both ‘wo’ and ‘wie’, and here it means how.

sentences.t: Do seh de Künigssuhn et gienge ünne gans schlechte, he sull sienen Kopp wohl mißen mutten: „dat Geschirr is mie wier klein gohen.“
sentences.l: Then said the king’s-son it went him quite badly, he should his head surely lose have to: “the gear is me again small gone.”
sentences.i: Then the king’s son said it was going very badly with him, he would surely have to lose his head: “the gear has gone to bits on me again.”
sentences.n: mißen = ‘missen’, to be without, to lose; sienen = ‘seinen’. klein gohen = ‘klein gehen’, to go to pieces. Geschirr here is his gear — the tools he was handed, not crockery. The dative mie is one of interest — “on me”.

sentences.t: „O,“ seh se, „he sull kummen un etten eest wat, dann werst du anneren Sinnes.“
sentences.l: “Oh,” said she, “he should come and eat first something, then become you of other mind.”
sentences.i: “Oh,” she said, “let him come and eat something first, and then you will be of another mind.”
sentences.n: She begins about him (he) and ends speaking to him (du) inside one sentence; the tale does this constantly and it is not a slip. anneren Sinnes is a genitive: ‘anderen Sinnes werden’.

sentences.t: „Nee,“ segd he, „etten kunn he nig, he wer gar to bedröwet.“
sentences.l: “No,” says he, “eat could he not, he were far too downcast.”
sentences.i: “No,” he said, “he could not eat, he was far too downcast.”
sentences.n: gar to = ‘gar zu’, far too. wer = ‘wäre’, the subjunctive that marks reported speech.

sentences.t: Do givt se ünne viel gude Woore bis he kummet un ett wat.
sentences.l: Then gives she him many good words until he comes and eats something.
sentences.i: Then she gave him so many fair words that at last he came and ate something.
sentences.n: gude Woore is the coaxing formula from the first task, back again with a different spelling of ‘gute’.

sentences.t: Do luset se ünn wier, un he schloppet in:
sentences.l: Then louses she him again, and he sleeps in:
sentences.i: Then she picked the lice from his head again, and he fell asleep:
sentences.n: ünn = ‘ihn’; the tale spells this pronoun ün, ünn and ünne without distinction.

sentences.t: se nümmet von niggen en Doock, schlett en Knupp do inne un kloppet mit den Knuppe dreimol up de Eere un segd „Arweggers, herut!“
sentences.l: she takes anew a cloth, strikes a knot into it and knocks with the knot three times on the earth and says “earth-workers, out here!”
sentences.i: she took a kerchief anew, tied a knot in it, and knocked three times with the knot on the ground, and said, “Earth-workers, come out!”
sentences.n: von niggen = ‘von neuem’, anew. schlett en Knupp = ‘schlägt einen Knoten’: one strikes a knot in Low German where English ties it. The summons is word for word the same as the first time.

sentences.t: Do kummt gliek so viele Eerdmännekens un froget olle wat ehr Begeren wür.
sentences.l: Then comes at once so many little earth-men and ask all what her desire were.
sentences.i: Then at once so many little earth-men came, and all asked what her desire was.
sentences.n: froget again is ‘fragen’, to ask. olle = ‘alle’ — this tale writes ‘alle’ that way throughout. Begeren = ‘Begehren’, desire; wür = ‘wäre’.

sentences.t: In Tied von drei Stunne mosten se den Dieck gans utschloen hewen, un he möste so blank sien, dann man sik inne speigelen künne, un von ollerhand Fiske mosten dorinne sien.
sentences.l: In time of three hours must they the pond quite dug out have, and it must so bright be, that one oneself in it mirror could, and of all kinds fish must therein be.
sentences.i: Within three hours they must have the pond dug quite out, and it must be so bright that one could see oneself in it, and there must be fish of every kind in it.
sentences.n: dann here stands for ‘dass’, opening a result clause. sik inne speigelen = ‘sich darin spiegeln’; inne is ‘darin’, in it.

sentences.t: Do giengen de Eerdmännekens hünn un boen ehre Verwanschap up, dat se ünnen helpen sullen; un et is auck in zwei Stunnen ferrig west.
sentences.l: Then went the little earth-men there and called their kindred up, that they them should help; and it is also in two hours finished been.
sentences.i: Then the little earth-men went off and called up their kindred to help them; and in two hours it was finished.
sentences.n: ünnen = ‘ihnen’; hünn = ‘hin’. Three hours were allowed and two sufficed — the tale keeps quietly raising the earth-men’s credit.

sentences.t: Do kummet se wier un seged „wie hät dohen, so us befolen is.“
sentences.l: Then come they again and said “we have done, as us commanded is.”
sentences.i: Then they came back and said, “We have done as we were bidden.”
sentences.n: wie hät = ‘wir haben’ — wie is ‘wir’ and hät is ‘haben’. dohen = ‘getan’; befolen = ‘befohlen’; so … is = ‘wie es … ist’.

sentences.t: Do nümmet de Künigsdochter den Doock un schlett wier dremol up de Eere un segd „Arweggers, to Hus!“
sentences.l: Then takes the king’s-daughter the cloth and strikes again three times on the earth and says “earth-workers, to house!”
sentences.i: Then the king’s daughter took the kerchief and struck three times on the ground again, and said, “Earth-workers, home!”
sentences.n: dremol here, dreimol elsewhere — one word, ‘dreimal’. to Hus = ‘zu Haus’.

sentences.t: Do siet se olle wier weg.
sentences.l: Then are they all again away.
sentences.i: And they were all gone again.
sentences.n: The same closing line as after the first task, one word shorter.

sentences.t: Ase do de Künigssuhn upwacket, do is de Dieck ferrig.
sentences.l: When then the king’s-son wakes up, there is the pond finished.
sentences.i: When the king’s son woke, the pond was finished.
sentences.n: upwacket and is are presents inside a past narrative — the tale switches tense without warning, and the English past is the natural rendering.

sentences.t: Do geit de Künigsdochter auck weg, un segd wenn et sesse wär, dann sull he nah Hus kummen.
sentences.l: Then goes the king’s-daughter also away, and says when it six were, then should he home come.
sentences.i: Then the king’s daughter went away too, and said that when it was six he should come home.
sentences.n: auck = ‘auch’. The reported speech takes wär and sull, subjunctives, exactly as High German would.

sentences.t: Ase he do nah Hus kummet, do frägt de Künig „hes du den Dieck ferrig?“
sentences.l: When he then home comes, then asks the king “have you the pond finished?”
sentences.i: When he came home, the king asked, “Have you the pond finished?”
sentences.n: hes = ‘hast’ — a still shorter form than hest a page earlier.

sentences.t: „Jo,“ seh de Künigssuhn.
sentences.l: “Yes,” said the king’s son.
sentences.n: seh here is ‘sagte’, said; the same three letters are ‘sehe’, I see, at the end of the tale.

sentences.t: Dat wür schöne.
sentences.l: That were fine.
sentences.i: That was well and good.
sentences.n: wür = ‘wäre’; schöne = ‘schön’. A one-line aside from the narrator — and the king is about to break his word again.

sentences.t: Do se do wier to Diske sittet, do seh de Künig „du hast den Dieck twaren ferrig, awerst ik kann die mine Dochter noch nie giewen, du most eest nau eins dohen.“
sentences.l: When they then again at table sit, then said the king “you have the pond indeed finished, but I can you my daughter still not give, you must first still one [thing] do.”
sentences.i: When they sat at table again, the king said, “You have the pond finished, true enough, but I still cannot give you my daughter; you must do one thing more first.”
sentences.n: noch nie = ‘noch nicht’, still not; nie is ‘nicht’ throughout this tale. eins is ‘eins’, one thing, and English needs the noun supplied, so it stands in square brackets in the literal line. to Diske = ‘zu Tische’.

sentences.t: „Wat is dat denn?“ frögte de Künigssuhn.
sentences.l: “What is that then?” asked the king’s-son.
sentences.n: frögte = ‘fragte’; denn is the flavouring particle that makes a question impatient rather than merely curious.

sentences.t: He hedde so en grot Berg, do würen luter Dorenbuske anne, de mosten olle afhoggen weren,
sentences.l: He had such a great mountain, there were nothing but thorn-bushes on it, those must all hewn down be,
sentences.i: He had a great mountain, he said, with nothing but thorn-bushes on it, and they must all be cut down,
sentences.n: The king’s words are reported with no ‘he said’ at all; the subjunctive hedde is what marks them. luter = ‘lauter’, nothing but; Dorenbuske = ‘Dornbüsche’; anne = ‘daran’, on it; weren = ‘werden’, the passive auxiliary.

sentences.t: un bowen up moste he en grot Schlott buggen, dat moste so wacker sien, ase’t nu en Menske denken kunne,
sentences.l: and above on it must he a great castle build, that must so handsome be, as it now a person imagine could,
sentences.i: and on the top he must build a great castle, and it must be as handsome as any person could imagine,
sentences.n: bowen = ‘oben’; buggen = ‘bauen’; wacker here is handsome, fine — not brave. ase’t = ase et, ‘als es’; Menske = ‘Mensch’.

sentences.t: un olle Ingedömse, de in den Schlott gehorden, de mösten der olle inne sien.
sentences.l: and all furnishings, which in the castle belonged, they must all in it be.
sentences.i: and all the furnishings that belong in a castle must all be in it.
sentences.n: Ingedömse is the household stuff and fittings of a house, High German ‘Hausgerät’; the word is rare and its exact reach is not certain. gehorden = ‘gehörten’; der is ‘da’, there.

sentences.t: Do he nu den anneren Morgen up steit, do gav ünne de Künig en glesernen Exen un en glesernen Boren mie: et mott awerst um sess Uhr ferrig sien.
sentences.l: When he now the next morning up stands, then gave him the king a glass axe and a glass auger along: it must however by six o’clock finished be.
sentences.i: When he got up the next morning, the king gave him a glass axe and a glass auger to take along — but it must be finished by six o’clock.
sentences.n: up steit = ‘aufsteht’; Boren = ‘Bohrer’, an auger; mie = ‘mit’, the particle of mitgeben. Three tasks, three sets of glass tools.

sentences.t: Do he an den eersten Dorenbuske mit de Exen anhogget, do gieng se so kurt un so klein dat de Stücker rund um ünne herfloen, un de Boren kunn he auck nig brucken.
sentences.l: When he at the first thorn-bush with the axe hews, there went it so short and so small that the pieces round about him flew, and the auger could he also not use.
sentences.i: When he struck at the first thorn-bush with the axe, it went to such small pieces that the splinters flew all round him, and the auger was no use to him either.
sentences.n: anhogget = ‘anhackt’; Stücker = ‘Stücke’; herfloen = ‘herflogen’; brucken = ‘brauchen’, here to use. so kurt un so klein comes back from the first task — the tale’s formula for smashed.

sentences.t: Do war he gans bedröwet un toffte (wartete) up sine Leiweste, op de nie keime un ünn ut de Naut hülpe.
sentences.l: Then was he quite downcast and waited for his dearest, whether she not would come and him out of the distress would help.
sentences.i: Then he was utterly downcast and waited for his dearest, wondering whether she would not come and help him out of his need.
sentences.n: toffte carries the Grimms’ own gloss, (wartete). Leiweste = ‘Liebste’, dearest — the first time the tale calls her so. op here is ‘ob’, whether, not ‘auf’; nie is ‘nicht’ again; Naut = ‘Not’ (1857 Noth), distress.

sentences.t: Ase’t do Middag is, do kummet se un bringet wat to etten:
sentences.l: When it then midday is, then comes she and brings something to eat:
sentences.i: When it was midday she came and brought something to eat:
sentences.n: bringet = ‘bringt’. The third task follows the first two step for step, and the tale abbreviates a little more each time.

sentences.t: do geit he ehr in de Möte (entgegen) un vertellt ehr olles un ett wat, un lett sik von ehr lusen un schloppet in.
sentences.l: there goes he her to meet and tells her everything and eats something, and lets himself by her be loused and sleeps in.
sentences.i: he went to meet her, and told her everything, and ate something, and let her pick the lice from his head, and fell asleep.
sentences.n: in de Möte gohen = ‘entgegengehen’, to go to meet — the Grimms gloss Möte as (entgegen). vertellt = ‘erzählt’; lett = ‘lässt’, lets — the same spelling means ‘looks’ elsewhere in Low German, but here it is the causative.

sentences.t: Do nümmetse wier den Knupp un schlett domit up de Eere un segd „Arweggers, herut!“
sentences.l: Then takes she again the knot and strikes with it on the earth and says “earth-workers, out here!”
sentences.i: Then she took the knot again and struck the ground with it, and said, “Earth-workers, come out!”
sentences.n: nümmetse is nümmet + se run together, ‘nimmt sie’; the 1857 text prints it as one word. domit = ‘damit’.

sentences.t: Do kummet wier so viel Eerdmännekens un froget wat ehr Begeren wür?
sentences.l: Then come again so many little earth-men and ask what her desire were?
sentences.i: Then so many little earth-men came again and asked what her desire was.
sentences.n: A reported question again, so the German keeps its question mark although nobody is being asked here. wür = ‘wäre’.

sentences.t: Do seh se „in Tied von drei Stunnen müttet ju den gansen Busk afhoggen,
sentences.l: Then said she “in time of three hours must you the whole thicket hew down,
sentences.i: Then she said, “Within three hours you must cut down the whole thicket,
sentences.n: müttet = ‘müsst’; ju = ‘ihr/euch’, here the plural you; Busk = ‘Busch’, the thorn thicket taken as one thing.

sentences.t: un bowen uppe den Berge do mot en Schlott stohen, dat mot so wacker sien, ase’t nu ener denken kann, un olle Ingedömse muttet do inne sien.“
sentences.l: and above upon the mountain there must a castle stand, it must so handsome be, as it now anyone imagine can, and all furnishings must in it be.”
sentences.i: and up on the mountain a castle must stand, as handsome as anyone could imagine, and all the furnishings must be in it.”
sentences.n: uppe = ‘oben auf’; ener = ‘einer’, anyone. She gives the king’s conditions back almost word for word — the tale’s way of showing that she has taken the whole task onto herself.

sentences.t: Do gienge se hünne un boen ehre Verwanschap up, dat se helpen sullen, un ase te Tied umme was, do was alles ferrig.
sentences.l: Then went they there and called their kindred up, that they should help, and when the time around was, then was everything finished.
sentences.i: Then they went off and called up their kindred to help, and when the time was up, everything was finished.
sentences.n: te here is the article ‘die’: te Tied = ‘die Zeit’. gienge = ‘gingen’; umme was = ‘um war’, was up.

sentences.t: Do kümmet se to der Künigsdochter un segged dat, un de Künigsdochter nümmet den Doock un schlett dreimol domit up de Eere un segd „Arweggers to Hus!“
sentences.l: Then come they to the king’s-daughter and say that, and the king’s-daughter takes the cloth and strikes three times with it on the earth and says “earth-workers, home!”
sentences.i: Then they came to the king’s daughter and told her so, and the king’s daughter took the kerchief and struck three times with it on the ground, and said, “Earth-workers, home!”
sentences.n: segged = ‘sagen (sie)’ — the tale has slipped into the narrative present here (kümmet, nümmet, schlett), so the form is present, not past. The dismissal formula stands for the third time, unchanged.

sentences.t: Do siet se glik olle wier weg west.
sentences.l: Then are they at once all again away been.
sentences.i: And at once they were all gone again.
sentences.n: glik = ‘gleich’, at once — spelled gliek a few lines earlier, and both spellings sit in the same paragraph.

sentences.t: Do nu de Künigssuhn upwecket, un olles soh, do was he so frau ase en Vugel in der Luft.
sentences.l: When now the king’s-son wakes up, and everything saw, then was he so glad as a bird in the air.
sentences.i: When the king’s son woke and saw it all, he was as glad as a bird in the air.
sentences.n: upwecket here for upwacket earlier; soh = ‘sah’; frau = ‘froh’. so frau ase en Vugel in der Luft is a set comparison, the kind of ready-made phrase these tales run on.

sentences.t: Do et do sesse schloen hadde, do giengen se tohaupe nah Hus.
sentences.l: When it then six struck had, then went they together home.
sentences.i: When it had struck six, they went home together.
sentences.n: tohaupe = ‘zuhauf, zusammen’, together — spelled tohope earlier in the tale.

sentences.t: Do segd de Künig „is dat Schlott auck ferrig?“
sentences.l: Then says the king “is the castle also finished?”
sentences.i: Then the king said, “Is the castle finished too?”
sentences.n: auck here carries a note of doubt: finished as well, is it.

sentences.t: „Jo“ seh de Künigssuhn.
sentences.l: “Yes,” said the king’s son.
sentences.n: The third bare Jo. Through this whole stretch the tale gives the young man almost no words of his own.

sentences.t: Ase do to Diske sittet, do segd de Künig „mine jungeste Dochter kann ik nie giewen, befur de twei öllesten frigget het.“
sentences.l: As [they] then at table sit, then says the king “my youngest daughter can I not give, before the two eldest married have.”
sentences.i: As they sat at table, the king said, “I cannot give my youngest daughter before the two eldest are married.”
sentences.n: The subject se is left out again and is supplied in square brackets in the literal line. befur = ‘bevor’; frigget = ‘gefreit’, married (freien). This is the fourth refusal, and the first that sets a condition he cannot work for.

sentences.t: Do wor de Künigssuhn un de Künigsdochter gans bedröwet, un de Künigssuhn wuste sik gar nig to bergen (helfen).
sentences.l: Then were the king’s-son and the king’s-daughter quite downcast, and the king’s-son knew himself not at all to help.
sentences.i: Then the king’s son and the king’s daughter were utterly downcast, and the king’s son was quite at a loss.
sentences.n: wor = ‘war/wurde’; wuste = ‘wusste’. sik nig to bergen weten is “not to know how to save oneself”, and the Grimms gloss bergen themselves as (helfen).

sentences.t: Do kummet he mol bie Nachte to der Künigsdochter un löppet dermit furt.
sentences.l: Then comes he once by night to the king’s-daughter and runs with that away.
sentences.i: Then one night he came to the king’s daughter, and off they ran together.
sentences.n: bie Nachte = ‘bei Nacht’; löppet = ‘läuft’; dermit = ‘damit’, with that, there and then; furt = ‘fort’.

sentences.t: Ase do en bitken wegsiet, do kicket sik de Dochter mol umme un süht ehren Vader hinner sik.
sentences.l: When [they] then a little bit away are, then looks the daughter once around and sees her father behind her.
sentences.i: When they were a little way off, the daughter looked round and saw her father behind them.
sentences.n: wegsiet = ‘weg sind’, are away — the subject is left out and supplied in brackets. sik ummekicken = ‘sich umgucken’, to look round; süht = ‘sieht’.

sentences.t: „O,“ seh se, „wo sull wie dat macken?
sentences.l: “Oh,” said she, “how shall we that make?
sentences.i: “Oh,” she said, “what shall we do?
sentences.n: wo is ‘wie’, how, and wie is ‘wir’, we — the two words look like each other’s translations and are not. macken = ‘machen’.

sentences.t: min Vader is hinner us un will us ummeholen:
sentences.l: my father is behind us and wants us to fetch back:
sentences.i: my father is behind us and means to fetch us back:
sentences.n: ummeholen = ‘umholen, zurückholen’, to fetch back.

sentences.t: ik will die grade to’n Dörenbusk macken un mie tor Rose un ik will mie ümmer midden in den Busk waaren (schützen).“
sentences.l: I will you straightway into a thorn-bush make and myself into the rose and I will myself always in the middle of the bush keep safe.”
sentences.i: I will turn you straightway into a thorn-bush and myself into the rose, and I will keep myself safe always in the middle of the bush.”
sentences.n: grade = ‘gerade’, straightway, on the spot; to’n = ‘zu einem’. waaren = ‘wahren’, to guard or keep safe, and the Grimms gloss it (schützen). The magic runs the other way from what a reader may expect: she transforms him, and he becomes the cover for her.

sentences.t: Ase do de Vader an de Stelle kummet, do steit do en Dörenbusk un ene Rose do anne:
sentences.l: When then the father to the place comes, there stands there a thorn-bush and a rose on it:
sentences.i: When the father came to the place, there stood a thorn-bush with a rose on it:
sentences.n: an de Stelle = ‘an die Stelle’, to the spot; anne = ‘daran’, on it.

sentences.t: do will he de Rose afbrecken, do kummet de Dören un stecket ün in de Finger, dat he wier nah Hus gehen mut.
sentences.l: there wants he the rose to break off, there comes the thorn and pricks him in the fingers, so that he again home go must.
sentences.i: he made to break off the rose, and the thorn came and pricked his fingers, so that he had to go home again.
sentences.n: Dören here is ‘Dorn’, thorn — not ‘Türen’, doors, which the same spelling means elsewhere. afbrecken = ‘abbrechen’; stecket = ‘sticht’.

sentences.t: Do frägt sine Frugge worumme he se nig hädde middebrocht.
sentences.l: Then asks his wife why he her not brought along had.
sentences.i: Then his wife asked why he had not brought her back with him.
sentences.n: worumme = ‘warum’; middebrocht = ‘mitgebracht’. The subjunctive hädde marks the whole thing as a reported question.

sentences.t: Do seh he he wür der balt bie west, awerst he hedde se uppen mol ut den Gesichte verloren, un do hädde do en Dörenbusk un ene Rose stohen.
sentences.l: Then said he he were there nearly by been, but he had her all at once out of the sight lost, and there had there a thorn-bush and a rose stood.
sentences.i: Then he said he had all but come up with them, but had lost sight of her all at once, and a thorn-bush with a rose on it had been standing there.
sentences.n: balt = ‘bald’, here nearly; der bie west = ‘dabei gewesen’, been right at them; uppen mol = ‘auf einmal’; ut den Gesichte verloren = ‘aus dem Gesicht verloren’, lost from sight.

sentences.t: Do seh de Künigin „heddest du ment (nur) de Rose afbrocken, de Busk hedde sullen wohl kummen.“
sentences.l: Then said the queen “had you only the rose broken off, the bush would surely have come.”
sentences.i: Then the queen said, “If you had only broken off the rose, the bush would have come along right enough.”
sentences.n: ment carries the Grimms’ own gloss, (nur), only. heddest du … is a conditional with no ‘wenn’, exactly as English says “had you only …”. hedde sullen … kummen = ‘hätte … kommen sollen’.

sentences.t: Do geit he wier weg un will de Rose herholen.
sentences.l: Then goes he again away and wants the rose to fetch.
sentences.i: Then he went off again to fetch the rose.
sentences.n: herholen = ‘herholen’, fetch here. He is sent back for a rose that is no longer there.

sentences.t: Unnerdes waren awerst de beiden schon wiet öwer Feld, un de Künig löppet der hinner her.
sentences.l: Meanwhile were however the two already far over field, and the king runs there behind after.
sentences.i: But meanwhile the two were already far across country, and the king ran after them.
sentences.n: Unnerdes = ‘unterdes’, meanwhile; wiet öwer Feld = ‘weit über Feld’, far across country; der hinner her = ‘da hinterher’.

sentences.t: Do kicket sik de Dochter wier umme un süht ehren Vader kummen: do seh se „o, wo sull wie et nu macken?
sentences.l: Then looks the daughter again around and sees her father coming: then said she “oh, how shall we it now make?
sentences.i: Then the daughter looked round again and saw her father coming, and she said, “Oh, what shall we do now?
sentences.n: The scene repeats the first pursuit in the same words; only the transformation will change.

sentences.t: ik will die grade tor Kerke macken un mie tom Pastoer: do will ik up de Kanzel stohn un predigen.“
sentences.l: I will you straightway into a church make and myself into the parson: there will I on the pulpit stand and preach.”
sentences.i: I will turn you straightway into a church and myself into the parson, and I will stand in the pulpit and preach.”
sentences.n: Kerke = ‘Kirche’; Pastoer = ‘Pastor’, the parson; Kanzel is the pulpit. Again she makes him the shell and herself the living thing inside it.

sentences.t: Ase do de Künig an de Stelle kummet, do steiht do ene Kerke, un up de Kanzel is en Pastoer un priediget:
sentences.l: When then the king to the place comes, there stands there a church, and on the pulpit is a parson and preaches:
sentences.i: When the king came to the place, there stood a church, and in the pulpit was a parson preaching:
sentences.n: priediget = ‘predigt’; the tale writes this word with the -ie- of Low German throughout, priedigen.

sentences.t: do hort he de Priedig to un geit wier nah Hus.
sentences.l: there listens he the sermon to and goes again home.
sentences.i: so he listened to the sermon and went home again.
sentences.n: Priedig = ‘Predigt’, sermon; tohören = ‘zuhören’, with the particle to standing at the end. The joke is a quiet one: the pursuing king sits through the whole sermon.

sentences.t: Do frägt de Küniginne worumme he se nig midde brocht hedde,
sentences.l: Then asks the queen why he her not along brought had,
sentences.i: Then the queen asked why he had not brought her along,
sentences.n: midde brocht here in two words, middebrocht in one a few lines earlier — the same verb, ‘mitbringen’.

sentences.t: da segd he „nee, ik hewe se so lange nachlaupen, un as ik glovte ik wer der bold bie, do steit do en Kerke un up de Kanzel en Pastoer, de priedigte.“
sentences.l: then says he “no, I have her so long run after, and as I believed I were there nearly by, there stands there a church and on the pulpit a parson, who preached.”
sentences.i: and he said, “No — I ran after her so long, and just as I thought I was almost up with her, there stood a church and in the pulpit a parson preaching.”
sentences.n: nachlaupen = ‘nachgelaufen’; glovte = ‘glaubte’; bold = ‘bald’, here nearly. The tense jumps into the present (steit) at the moment of surprise; that is how this tale marks a shock.

sentences.t: „Du häddest sullen ment den Pastoer bringen,“ seh de Fru,
sentences.l: “You should only the parson brought have,” said the woman,
sentences.i: “You should have brought only the parson,” said his wife,
sentences.n: häddest sullen … bringen = ‘hättest … bringen sollen’; Low German puts the three parts in a different order from High German. Fru = ‘Frau’, here the queen as wife.

sentences.t: „de Kerke hädde sullen wohl kummen: dat ik die auck (wenn ich dich auch) schicke, dat kann nig mer helpen, ik mut sülwenst hünne gohen.“
sentences.l: “the church would surely have come: that I you as well send, that can not more help, I must myself over go.”
sentences.i: “the church would have followed right enough. It is no use my sending you again — I must go over myself.”
sentences.n: The Grimms supply their own gloss here in round brackets, (wenn ich dich auch), because dat ik die auck schicke is hard even in Low German: literally “that I send you as well”. mer = ‘mehr’; hünne gohen = ‘hingehen’.

sentences.t: Ase se do ene Wiele wege is un de beiden von fern süht, do kicket sik de Künigsdochter umme un süht ehre Moder kummen
sentences.l: When she then a while away is and the two from afar sees, then looks the king’s-daughter around and sees her mother coming
sentences.i: When she had been on the way a while and saw the two from afar, the king’s daughter looked round and saw her mother coming
sentences.n: Wiele = ‘Weile’; wege = ‘weg’; ehre = ‘ihre’. The queen goes herself, and the tale accordingly makes the third pursuit the dangerous one.

sentences.t: un segd „nu si wie unglücksk, nu kummet miene Moder sülwenst: ik will die grade tom Dieck macken un mie tom Fisk.“
sentences.l: and says “now are we unlucky, now comes my mother herself: I will you straightway into the pond make and myself into the fish.”
sentences.i: and said, “Now we are lost — now my mother comes herself. I will turn you straightway into the pond and myself into the fish.”
sentences.n: si wie = ‘sind wir’; unglücksk = ‘unglücklich’; miene = ‘meine’, my — not ‘Miene’, a look. Third transformation, and for the third time she is the small live thing inside the big still one.

sentences.t: Do de Moder up de Stelle kummet, do is do en grot Dieck,
sentences.l: When the mother to the place comes, there is there a great pond,
sentences.i: When the mother came to the place, there was a great pond,
sentences.n: up de Stelle here, an de Stelle for the father a few lines back — the tale is not consistent about its prepositions.

sentences.t: un in de Midde sprank en Fisk herumme un kickete mit den Kopp ut den Water un was gans lustig.
sentences.l: and in the middle sprang a fish about and peeped with the head out of the water and was quite merry.
sentences.i: and in the middle a fish was leaping about, putting its head out of the water, and was very merry.
sentences.n: sprank = ‘sprang’; kickete = ‘guckte’, peeped; lustig here means lively, in high spirits.

sentences.t: Do wull se geren den Fisk krigen, awerst se kunn ün gar nig fangen.
sentences.l: Then wanted she gladly the fish to get, but she could it not at all catch.
sentences.i: She would gladly have had the fish, but she could not catch it at all.
sentences.n: geren = ‘gern’; krigen = ‘kriegen’, to get; gar nig = ‘gar nicht’, not at all.

sentences.t: Do werd se gans böse un drinket den gansen Dieck ut, dat se den Fisk kriegen will,
sentences.l: Then becomes she quite angry and drinks the whole pond out, so that she the fish get may,
sentences.i: Then she grew quite angry and drank the whole pond dry, so as to get the fish,
sentences.n: gansen = ‘ganzen’; utdrinken with the particle ut standing at the end. gans is ‘ganz’ throughout this tale, never a goose.

sentences.t: awerst do werd se so üwel, dat se sick spiggen mott un spigget den gansen Dieck wier ut.
sentences.l: but then becomes she so sick, that she herself vomit must and spews the whole pond again out.
sentences.i: but then she grew so sick that she had to be ill, and spewed the whole pond up again.
sentences.n: üwel = ‘übel’, sick; sick spiggen = ‘sich speien’, to vomit. The tale is not squeamish, and the translation follows it.

sentences.t: Do seh se „ik sehe do wohl dat et olle nig mer helpen kann:“
sentences.l: Then said she “I see indeed that it all no more help can:”
sentences.i: Then she said, “I see well enough that none of it is any use any more:”
sentences.n: Here sehe really is ‘sehe’, I see — three lines after seh meant ‘sagte’. Only the sentence around them tells the two apart. mer = ‘mehr’.

sentences.t: sei mogten nu wier to ehr kummen.
sentences.l: they might now again to her come.
sentences.i: they might come back to her now.
sentences.n: sei is ‘sie’, they. The queen’s surrender is reported with no ‘she said’ at all; mogten = ‘möchten’.

sentences.t: Do gohet se dann auck wier hünne, un de Küniginne givt der Dochter drei Wallnütte un segd „do kannst du die mit helpen, wenn du in dine högste Naud bist.“
sentences.l: Then go they then also again over, and the queen gives the daughter three walnuts and says “there can you yourself with help, when you in your greatest need are.”
sentences.i: So they went back to her, and the queen gave the daughter three walnuts and said, “With these you can help yourself when you are in your greatest need.”
sentences.n: Wallnütte = ‘Walnüsse’; högste = ‘höchste’; Naud = ‘Not’ (1857 Noth). The three nuts are the only gift in the tale, and they pay for the whole of the ending.

sentences.t: Un do giengen de jungen Lüde wier tohaupe weg.
sentences.l: And then went the young folk again together away.
sentences.i: And then the young people went off together again.
sentences.n: Lüde here, Lude at the start of the tale: the same word, ‘Leute’.

sentences.t: Do se do wohl tein Stunne gohen hadden, do kummet se an dat Schlott, wovon de Künigssuhn was, un dobie was en Dorp.
sentences.l: When they then a good ten hours gone had, then come they to the castle, of which the king’s-son was, and beside it was a village.
sentences.i: When they had walked a good ten hours, they came to the castle the king’s son belonged to, and there was a village beside it.
sentences.n: tein = ‘zehn’; Stunne here is a stretch of walking as much as a clock-hour. wovon de Künigssuhn was = whose he was; dobie = ‘dabei’, beside it.

sentences.t: Ase se do anne keimen, do segd de Künigssuhn „blief hie, mine Leiweste, ik will eest up dat Schlott gohen,
sentences.l: When they then there arrived, then says the king’s-son “stay here, my dearest, I will first up to the castle go,
sentences.i: When they came up, the king’s son said, “Stay here, my dearest; I will go up to the castle first,
sentences.n: anne keimen = ‘ankamen’, arrived; blief = ‘bleib’, stay; hie = ‘hier’.

sentences.t: un dann will ik mit den Wagen un Bedeinten kummen un will die afholen.“
sentences.l: and then will I with the carriage and servants come and will you fetch.”
sentences.i: and then I will come with the carriage and servants and fetch you.”
sentences.n: Bedeinten = ‘Bedienten’, servants; afholen = ‘abholen’, to fetch. The promise is exact — and it is exactly what the kiss will wipe out.

sentences.t: Ase he do up dat Schlott kummet, do werd se olle so frau dat se den Künigssuhn nu wier hett:
sentences.l: When he then up to the castle comes, there become they all so glad that they the king’s-son now again have:
sentences.i: When he came up to the castle, they were all so glad to have the king’s son back again:
sentences.n: se olle = ‘sie alle’; hett = ‘hat, haben’; frau is ‘froh’ once more.

sentences.t: do vertellt he he hedde ene Brut, un de wür ietzt in den Dorpe, se wullen mit den Wagen hintrecken un se holen.
sentences.l: there tells he he had a bride, and she were now in the village, they wanted with the carriage over to drive and her fetch.
sentences.i: and he told them he had a bride, and she was now down in the village, and they should drive over with the carriage and fetch her.
sentences.n: Brut = ‘Braut’; ietzt = ‘jetzt’; hintrecken = ‘hinziehen’, to set off over there. The whole sentence is reported speech and keeps its subjunctives, hedde, wür, wullen.

sentences.t: Do spannt se auck gliek an, un viele Bedeinten setten sich up den Wagen.
sentences.l: Then harness they also at once up, and many servants set themselves on the carriage.
sentences.i: So they harnessed up at once, and many servants took their places on the carriage.
sentences.n: anspannen, to put the horses to; the particle an stands at the end. setten sich = ‘setzten sich’.

sentences.t: Ase do de Künigssuhn instiegen wull, do gab ün sine Moder en Kus, do hadde he alles vergeten, wat schehen was un auck wat he dohen will.
sentences.l: When then the king’s-son to get in wanted, there gave him his mother a kiss, then had he everything forgotten, what happened was and also what he to do meant.
sentences.i: Just as the king’s son was about to get in, his mother gave him a kiss, and at once he had forgotten everything — what had happened, and what he meant to do.
sentences.n: instiegen = ‘einsteigen’; Kus = ‘Kuss’; schehen = ‘geschehen’. The forgetting-kiss turns up all over the collection. Nothing is said here about the mother meaning harm, and the tale never explains it.

sentences.t: Do befal de Moder se sullen wier utspannen, un do giengen se olle wier in’t Hus.
sentences.l: Then commanded the mother they should again unharness, and then went they all again into the house.
sentences.i: Then the mother ordered them to unharness again, and they all went back into the house.
sentences.n: befal = ‘befahl’; utspannen = ‘ausspannen’, the exact opposite of the anspannen two lines above.

sentences.t: Dat Mäken awerst sitt im Dorpe un luert un luert un meint he sull se afholen, et kummet awerst keiner.
sentences.l: The girl however sits in the village and waits and waits and thinks he should her fetch, there comes however no one.
sentences.i: But the girl sat in the village and waited and waited, thinking he would come and fetch her; but no one came.
sentences.n: luert = ‘lauert’, waits on the watch; meint = ‘meint’, thinks; et kummet awerst keiner = ‘es kommt aber keiner’. Mäken is a neuter noun, and from here on the tale will often call the girl et, ‘it’, following the grammar rather than the person.

sentences.t: Do vermaiet (vermiethet) sik de Künigsdochter in de Muhle, de hoerde bie dat Schlott, do moste se olle Nohmiddage bie den Watter sitten un Stunze schüren (Gefäße reinigen).
sentences.l: Then hires the king’s-daughter herself out into the mill, which belonged to the castle, there must she all afternoons by the water sit and vessels scour.
sentences.i: Then the king’s daughter hired herself out at the mill, which belonged to the castle, and there she had to sit by the water every afternoon and scour the vessels.
sentences.n: The Grimms gloss two of their own words here: vermaiet as (vermiethet), hires herself out, and Stunze schüren as (Gefäße reinigen), to scour the vessels. Watter = ‘Wasser’; Nohmiddage = ‘Nachmittage’. A king’s daughter at the washing-place is her lowest point in the tale.

sentences.t: Do kummet de Küniginne mol von den Schlotte gegohen, un gohet an den Water spatzeiern, un seihet dat wackere Mäken do sitten,
sentences.l: Then comes the queen once from the castle walking, and goes by the water strolling, and sees the fair girl there sitting,
sentences.i: One day the queen came walking down from the castle, and strolled along by the water, and saw the fair girl sitting there,
sentences.n: gegohen kummen = ‘gegangen kommen’, to come walking — a past participle with kommen, just as High German has it. spatzeiern = ‘spazieren’; wackere here is comely, handsome.

sentences.t: do segd se „wat is dat für en wacker Mäken! wat geföllt mie dat gut!“
sentences.l: there says she “what is that for a fair girl! how pleases me that well!”
sentences.i: and she said, “What a fair girl that is! How well I like her!”
sentences.n: wat … für = ‘was für’, what a; the second wat is ‘wie’, how; geföllt = ‘gefällt’. The queen admires the girl she has kept from her son, and does not know her.

sentences.t: Do kicket se et olle an, awerst keen Menske hadde et kand.
sentences.l: Then look they it all at, but no person had it known.
sentences.i: Then they all looked at her, but nobody knew her.
sentences.n: et for the girl again — the neuter of Mäken. kand = ‘gekannt’; keen = ‘kein’; Menske = ‘Mensch’.

sentences.t: Do geit wohl ene lange Tied vorbie, dat dat Mäken eerlick un getrugge bie den Müller deint.
sentences.l: Then goes a good long time by, that the girl honestly and faithfully at the miller’s serves.
sentences.i: A good long time went by, and all that while the girl served the miller honestly and faithfully.
sentences.n: eerlick = ‘ehrlich’; getrugge = ‘getreu’; deint = ‘dient’. dat here is ‘dass’, opening a clause of duration.

sentences.t: Unnerdes hadde de Küniginne ene Frugge für ehren Suhn socht, de is gans feren ut der Weld west.
sentences.l: Meanwhile had the queen a wife for her son sought, who is quite far out of the world been.
sentences.i: Meanwhile the queen had sought out a wife for her son, who came from quite far out in the world.
sentences.n: socht = ‘gesucht’; feren = ‘fern’; Weld = ‘Welt’. gans feren ut der Weld means only that she came from very far off.

sentences.t: Ase do de Brut ankümmet, do söllt se gliek tohaupe giewen weren.
sentences.l: When then the bride arrives, then shall they at once together given be.
sentences.i: When the bride arrived, they were to be married at once.
sentences.n: tohaupe giewen weren = ‘zusammengegeben werden’, to be given together, i.e. married. ankümmet = ‘ankommt’.

sentences.t: Et laupet so viele Lüde tosamen, de dat olle seihen willt, do segd dat Mäken to den Müller he mögte ehr doch auck Verlöv giewen.
sentences.l: There run so many folk together, who that all see want, then says the girl to the miller he might her too leave give.
sentences.i: So many people came running together, all wanting to see it, that the girl said to the miller he might give her leave as well.
sentences.n: willt here is ‘wollen’, third person plural. Verlöv = ‘Verlaub, Erlaubnis’, leave; mögte = ‘möchte’, the polite subjunctive of a request.

sentences.t: Do seh de Müller „goh menten hünne.“
sentences.l: Then said the miller “go only over.”
sentences.i: Then the miller said, “Go along, then.”
sentences.n: menten = ‘nur denn’, only, just — a little cluster of Low German particles; the Grimms glossed the shorter ment as (nur) earlier in the tale.

sentences.t: Ase’t do weg will, do macket et ene van den drei Wallnütten up, do legt do so en wacker Kleid inne,
sentences.l: When it then away will, then opens it one of the three walnuts up, there lies there such a fair dress inside,
sentences.i: When she was about to set off, she opened one of the three walnuts, and there lay such a fair dress inside,
sentences.n: et is the girl — Mäken is neuter. van = ‘von’. legt here is ‘liegt’, lies, not ‘legt’, lays; the two verbs fall together in this spelling and only the sense tells them apart. upmacken = ‘aufmachen’, with the particle up at the end.

sentences.t: dat trecket et an un gienk domie in de Kerke gigen den Altor stohen.
sentences.l: that puts it on and went with it into the church up to the altar to stand.
sentences.i: she put it on and went in it into the church, and took her stand before the altar.
sentences.n: antrecken = ‘anziehen’, to put on. gigen den Altor = ‘gegen den Altar’, up at the altar. gienk = ‘ging’; domie = ‘damit’, in it.

sentences.t: Up enmol kummt de Brut un de Brüme (Bräutigam), un settet sik für den Altor,
sentences.l: All at once comes the bride and the bridegroom, and set themselves before the altar,
sentences.i: All at once the bride and the bridegroom came, and took their places before the altar,
sentences.n: Brüme carries the Grimms’ own gloss, (Bräutigam). enmol = ‘einmal’; für = ‘vor’, before.

sentences.t: un ase de Pastor se do insegnen wull, do kicket sik de Brut van der Halwe (seitwärts), un süht et do stohen,
sentences.l: and when the parson them then bless would, then looks the bride from the side, and sees it there standing,
sentences.i: and when the parson was about to bless them, the bride glanced aside and saw her standing there,
sentences.n: insegnen = ‘einsegnen’, to bless, to solemnise a marriage. van der Halwe is glossed by the Grimms, (seitwärts) — from the side.

sentences.t: do steit se wier up, un segd se wull sik nie giewen loten, bis se auck so en wacker Kleid hädde, ase de Dame.
sentences.l: there stands she again up, and says she would herself not give let, until she also such a fair dress had, as the lady.
sentences.i: and she stood up again and said she would not let herself be married until she had a fair dress like the lady’s.
sentences.n: sik giewen loten = ‘sich geben lassen’, to let oneself be given in marriage. nie is ‘nicht’ once more. Dame is a French loanword and the only smart word in the tale: the bride sees a lady, not a mill-maid.

sentences.t: Do giengen se wier nah Hus un läten de Dame froen ob se dat Kleid wohl verkofte.
sentences.l: Then went they again home and let the lady be asked whether she the dress perhaps would sell.
sentences.i: Then they went home again and had the lady asked whether she would sell the dress.
sentences.n: läten … froen = ‘ließen … fragen’, had her asked; verkofte = ‘verkaufte’, a subjunctive in the reported question. wohl softens it, as English “would she perhaps”.

sentences.t: Nee, verkaupen dau se’t nig, awerst verdeinen, dat mögte wohl sien.
sentences.l: No, sell do she it not, but earn, that might well be.
sentences.i: No, sell it she would not; but earn it — that might well be.
sentences.n: dau se’t = ‘tue sie es’ — Low German uses dohn as a helping verb the way older English uses “do”. verdeinen = ‘verdienen’, to earn: she will not sell the dress, but she will let it be earned. Her answer is reported with no ‘she said’.

sentences.t: Do fragten se ehr wat se denn dohen sullen.
sentences.l: Then asked they her what they then to do should.
sentences.i: Then they asked her what they should do, then.
sentences.n: ehr = ‘ihr’, her; both instances of se are ‘sie’, they, the people from the castle.

sentences.t: Do segd se wenn se van Nachte fur dat Dohr van den Künigssuhn schlapen döffte, dann wull se et wohl dohen.
sentences.l: Then says she if she of nights before the door of the king’s-son sleep might, then would she it surely do.
sentences.i: Then she said that if she might sleep by night before the king’s son’s door, she would do it willingly.
sentences.n: van Nachte = ‘des Nachts’, by night; Dohr = ‘Thür, Tür’, door; döffte = ‘dürfte’. She names the only price she wants.

sentences.t: Do seged se jo, dat sul se menten dohen.
sentences.l: Then said they yes, that should she just do.
sentences.i: Then they said yes, she might do that and welcome.
sentences.n: sul = ‘sollte’; menten again, only, just. They agree without a thought — nobody at the castle knows what she is.

sentences.t: Do muttet de Bedeinten den Künigssuhn en Schlopdrunk ingiewen, un do legt se sik up den Süll un günselt (winselt) de heile Nacht,
